name: Vera Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for agreeing to talk, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and what you say is confidential. To begin, could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a roof bolter at the potash mine, underground, about a kilometre down. Potash is a salt they use in fertiliser. After the cutting machine goes through, I drive the bolter in and drill long steel bolts up into the roof so it doesn't come down on anyone. My father has worked at this mine for thirty-one years and my brother Karim is on the conveyors, so I grew up hearing about the place at dinner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing my work keeps people safe. When I put in a good row of bolts I think of my father walking under them. The hard part is I'm slow, still learning, and the shift boss checks my rows twice. I live at home and pay my parents board, and I help with my grandmother's medicine, so whatever's left at the end of the month is mostly a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read five pictures of the future and ask about each. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Most of what people get excited about comes and goes. My father has seen three 'new systems' come into the mine and two of them went in the bin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay as they are, which is what I want. I'm not someone who likes change for its own sake. I want to get good at this, and maybe in a few years be married and still working here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Go to work, pay board, help with Grandma's medicine. Try to put a little aside for a wedding one day, though there's no one to marry yet, my mother would like me to say that clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two of the three new systems went in the bin. What were they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One was a tracking tag on your helmet that kept losing signal underground, everyone hated it. The other was some computer that was supposed to plan the cutting, and the old shift bosses just ignored it until it went away. The one that stayed was the new ventilation, because it actually worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself, on your phone or anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Karim talks to one on his phone like it's a friend, I think it's strange. If I want to know something I ask my father or I ask at the mine.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because most exciting new things come and go. My father has seen three new systems arrive at the mine and two were thrown out.
S0.think: I think it means things stay as they are, which is what I want. I'd like to get good at this job, maybe marry in a few years, and still work here.
S0.do: Carries on working, paying board to her parents and helping with her grandmother's medicine. Hopes to put a little aside towards a wedding one day.
S0.quote: My father has seen three 'new systems' come into the mine and two of them went in the bin.
S0.fieldNote: Her family history at the mine gives her a long view of technology that fails. She values continuity and doesn't use AI tools at all. Her money goes to family, which she sees as normal rather than a burden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has the right to run its business how it wants, that's how it works. But I'd also say a good company remembers the families who built it. I'd say that at home, not online, I don't do online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I know they already have bolters that do most of it themselves at some mines, with one person watching. I'm the slow new one. If they need fewer bolter operators, I'm the one who goes, and it would shame me in front of my father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder and cleaner than anyone, so they have no reason. I'd ask my father to speak to the people he knows. I'd stop buying anything that isn't needed. I wouldn't sign up for courses about computers, I'd rather wait and see if it really comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, and embarrassed to be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it would shame you in front of your father. Why shame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he got me the start. He told the foreman I'd work hard. If I'm the first one let go, it says something about him too. That's how it feels, even if it's silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some would ask the government for help in that position. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not first. First family, then the community at our mosque, they help people find work. Government money is for people who truly can't. I'd rather take a cleaning job than sit and wait for a payment.

S1.say: I'd say the company has the right to run its business as it wants, but a good company remembers the families who built it. I'd say that at home rather than online.
S1.think: I think bolters that mostly run themselves already exist, and as the slow new one I'd go first. It would shame me in front of my father, who got me the start.
S1.do: Works harder and cleaner so there's no reason to let her go and asks her father to speak to his contacts. Cuts all unneeded spending and waits to see if the change really comes rather than taking computer courses.
S1.feel: Worried, and embarrassed to be worried.
S1.quote: If I'm the first one let go, it says something about him too.
S1.fieldNote: Her fear is tied to family honour more than money, because her father vouched for her. She defends the company's right to automate while expecting loyalty from it. She'd turn to family and her mosque community long before the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people shouldn't panic and families should stick together. I don't think the government can fix this with money, it'll just make everyone dependent. I'd want them to protect real jobs somehow, but I don't know how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years, my father, my brother and me, all three of us could be out of the mine together. That's the whole household income. And my grandmother's medicine doesn't stop because the robots came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any extra shifts while they still exist and put everything aside. I'd look for any work that still needs a person, a shop, cleaning, the care home where my aunt works. The family would pool everything, we'd cut down to one car. If it came to it, I'd accept the government help, but I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray a lot. I'd be scared for my parents more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate taking government help. What would make it easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it felt like it was paid back somehow. Like work for the town, fixing things, helping the old people. Then it's not a handout, it's a job by another name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make him tea. He doesn't talk about feelings, so I'd ask him about the old days at the mine and let him tell the stories. Then after he went to bed I'd sit with my mother and we'd do the numbers.

S2.say: I'd say people shouldn't panic and families should stick together. I don't think government money fixes this, though I'd want real jobs protected somehow.
S2.think: I think my father, my brother and I could all be out of the mine together within two years, which is the whole household income. My grandmother's medicine won't stop because robots came.
S2.do: Takes extra shifts while they last and saves everything, then looks for any job that still needs a person, such as cleaning or care work. Pools money with the family, cuts to one car, and reluctantly accepts government help if needed.
S2.feel: Frightened, mostly for her parents, and praying a lot.
S2.quote: Like work for the town, fixing things, helping the old people. Then it's not a handout, it's a job by another name.
S2.fieldNote: The scale of the threat is the family's, not just hers: three incomes from one mine. Her reluctance about government help softens if it comes as work for the town. The night-of scene with tea and stories was very specific and affecting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so families and the community should get ready together, and companies should keep apprenticeships going. That's what built this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. My father would be close to retiring anyway, so maybe that's lucky for him. For me, I'd be thirty-two and only know bolting. I don't know what I'd do. I don't have a plan, and I don't like that I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and wait a year or two to see if it's really coming. If it is, I'd ask about an apprenticeship that still needs hands, maybe plumbing, my uncle is a plumber in the next town. And I'd save what I can for the family, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like hearing a rock creak above you, you don't know when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A plumbing apprenticeship would mean a pay cut. Could you manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only living at home. That's the good thing about living with my parents, they'd say 'stay, eat, learn.' My uncle would teach me, family looks after family. But robots doing hands-on work means plumbing too, eventually, doesn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So why plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's in houses, under sinks, in old buildings. I think it's the last place they'd send a robot. And because I know my uncle. I'd rather learn from someone I trust than a computer course.

S3.say: I'd say we have a few years, so families and the community should get ready together and companies should keep apprenticeships going. That's what built this town.
S3.think: I think my father might be close enough to retirement to be lucky, but I'd be thirty-two and only know bolting. I don't have a plan, and I don't like that.
S3.do: Keeps working and waits a year or two to see if it's coming, then looks at a plumbing apprenticeship with her uncle while living at home. Saves what she can for the family.
S3.feel: Anxious, like hearing a rock creak above her without knowing when it will fall.
S3.quote: It's like hearing a rock creak above you, you don't know when.
S3.fieldNote: She wants an apprenticeship from someone she trusts, not a course, which fits her traditional outlook. Living at home makes a pay cut possible. She noticed herself that plumbing isn't safe forever either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for a family to plan, so plan. Don't wait for someone else to fix it. I'd say it to my cousins, the younger ones especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I can maybe accept. My father would be retired, my grandmother, I hope she's still with us, but who knows. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe married, maybe not. I'd have time to learn a trade from my uncle properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the mine for now and only start the plumbing apprenticeship when I see the first robot bolter on our level. I'd save a little each month for a wedding, if there's a wedding. I'd keep doing what I do well until the day it isn't needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can pray about it and wait. That feels possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait until you see a robot bolter on your level. Is that cutting it close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've seen people jump early and lose everything. Better one sure step than three nervous ones. My father says that about bolting too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if ten years went by and the town wasn't ready?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the company, they did what businesses do. The schools, maybe, for not teaching trades anymore. And families who didn't talk to each other about it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for a family to plan, so plan and don't wait for someone else to fix it. I'd tell my younger cousins especially.
S4.think: I think I can maybe accept ten years, because my father would be retired and I'd have time to learn a trade from my uncle properly. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe married, maybe not.
S4.do: Stays at the mine and only starts a plumbing apprenticeship once she sees a robot bolter on her own level. Saves a little each month towards a possible wedding.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but able to pray about it and wait.
S4.quote: Better one sure step than three nervous ones.
S4.fieldNote: The decade lets her stay true to her cautious nature, and she frames it with her father's bolting wisdom. She doesn't blame the company at all, pointing instead to schools and families. Faith gives her a way to sit with uncertainty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes my father, my brother and me at the same time. What would help is apprenticeships that still pay a little, and companies that give the old families first chance at whatever work is left. Not a cheque in the post. Work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the mine means to the town. It's not only wages. It's the football team, the Christmas party, my father's friends. A robot doesn't buy raffle tickets.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't buy raffle tickets.
portrait: Vera Rahman is a 27-year-old junior roof bolter a kilometre underground at a potash mine, where her father has worked for thirty-one years and her brother runs the conveyors. She lives at home, pays board, helps with her grandmother's medicine and has almost nothing saved. Cautious and traditional, she doesn't use AI tools, defends the company's right to run its business and would turn to family and her mosque community before the government. The two-year picture frightens her because it could take three family incomes at once, while with more time she'd wait for proof and then learn plumbing from her uncle.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because it could take her father's, her brother's and her own jobs at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships that still pay a little, and companies giving long-serving families first chance at whatever work is left, rather than a cheque in the post.
